The eggs of the White-bearded hermit (Phaethornis hispidus) require a relatively brief incubation period before the altricial nestlings emerge. Field observations indicate that within nests maintained at an ambient temperature of 26 °C [T = 26 °C], the developing chicks hatch after approximately 16 days [ab = approximately 16 days], a duration typical for small-bodied tropical hummingbirds. Upon hatching, these altricial chicks are remarkably underdeveloped, with an initial wet body mass of just 0.7 grams [Ww0 = 0.7 grams], a value representing a small fraction of the ultimate female adult mass. This minuscule size at emergence places a high demand on the provisioning capabilities of the attending adult, as the nestlings must undergo a rapid and energy-intensive growth trajectory. The naked, blind neonates are entirely dependent on the brooding parent for thermoregulation and on regurgitated arthropods and nectar provided by the female. During these first few days post-hatching, the chick's weight increases dramatically as yolk reserves are depleted and exogenous feeding commences, setting the stage for the subsequent developmental milestones that will prepare the individual for eventual independence.

As the nestling develops, key physiological and morphological milestones are reached under the elevated body temperatures characteristic of active hummingbirds, typically around 38.1 °C [T = 38.1 °C]. At this internal temperature, the young bird achieves the capacity for sustained flight, known as fledging, at approximately 21 days after hatching [tx = approximately 21 days after hatching], although the precise timing can vary within a narrow window of at a temperature of 38.1 °C [T = 38.1 °C] 20 to 22 days. Reaching this developmental benchmark marks the transition from a sedentary, nest-dependent chick to a mobile fledgling capable of making short flights. Following fledging, the individual continues to mature, with the onset of reproductive maturity occurring considerably later. Puberty, defined as the attainment of full gonadal development, is reached around 63 days after hatching [tp = around 63 days after hatching] when maintained at this same typical body temp at a temperature of 38.1 °C [T = 38.1 °C]erature.

Reproduction in the White-bearded hermit follows a highly constrained annual schedule, reflecting the energetic limitations of a small, metabolically active nectarivore. Females typically produce a single clutch per year [F_R_i = single clutch per year], a low frequency that is compensated for by the production of two eggs per clutch [N_R_i = two eggs per clutch]. This annual reproductive output is modest compared to many passerines, but it aligns with the slow life-history pace common among hummingbirds, where high metabolic costs and territory defense limit the energy available for offspring production. The first breeding event, or the age at which a female lays her first brood, occurs at about 365 days since birth [tR = about 365 days since birth], a full year after her own hatching, under the thermal regime of 38.1 °C [T = 38.1 °C]. This delay between reaching puberty and initiating reproduction is likely an adaptive strategy, allowing the young female to accumulate sufficient body condition and establish a feeding territory that can support the demands of egg formation and subsequent chick provisioning. The entire reproductive cycle is thus tightly synchronized with local resource peaks.

Longevity in this species, while difficult to assess in the wild due to high juvenile mortality, has been estimated from banding studies. Under the typical active body temperature of 38.1 °C [T = 38.1 °C], the maximum recorded lifespan for a White-bearded hermit is approximately 7.3 years [am = approximately 7.3 years], with some individuals potentially reaching up to 8 years. This lifespan is comparatively long for a bird of its diminutive size, which typically exhibits a negative correlation between body mass and longevity. The extended lifespan is likely facilitated by a low extrinsic mortality risk associated with its relatively stable tropical environment and a specialized, low-competition foraging niche. Furthermore, the high metabolic costs of hovering flight are offset by periods of torpor, which help conserve energy and reduce oxidative damage over the long term. This life-history strategy, characterized by a single, small clutch per year and a delayed first reproduction, is consistent with a "slow" pace of life, where adult survival is prioritized over high annual reproductive output to ensure lifetime fitness.

The basal metabolic rate of the White-bearded hermit provides a physiological window into its energetic ecology. Respirometry trials have measured a maximum resting oxygen consumption of 25.45 milliliters of oxygen per hour [JOi = 25.45 milliliters of oxygen per hour] when the bird is in its thermoneutral zone and at a body temperature of 38.1 °C [T = 38.1 °C]. This value, while elevated relative to other bird families, is generally consistent with the high mass-specific metabolic rates documented in other hummingbirds, reflecting the immense energetic cost of their specialized hovering flight and rapid wingbeat frequencies. Comparatively, this measured rate is near the upper limit for a bird of the ultimate wet weight typically observed for adult females, which is approximately 5 grams [Wwi = approximately 5 grams]. The close coupling between a high metabolic rate, a small body size, and a nectarivorous diet imposes a strict energetic budget, requiring the bird to visit hundreds of flowers daily to meet its caloric requirements. This physiological constraint ultimately shapes nearly every aspect of its behavior, from its solitary foraging habits to its seasonal breeding schedule.
